statements.text: We are in a competition here, right. We are in a competition. We do not want to cede this space to China. How do we keep up with them or, you know, maintain a lead in this area and ethically do due diligence in terms of our obligation to protect privacy rights and, you know, democratic ideals?
statements.context: House Oversight Committee hearing on using cutting-edge technologies to keep America safe, where Rep. Lynch questions panelists about the AI competition with China and Russia.

statements.text: This Executive Order directs the Treasury to draft regulations that require disclosure of or prohibit certain outbound foreign investments into mainland China, to Hong Kong, or to Macau. [...] it only covers certain aspects of advanced computing, quantum information technologies, and AI, and that other activity, including financial investment, might not be covered. [...] if there are any gaps that you recognize that might be covered, just to give Congress an idea of what direction we might be looking at.
statements.context: Congressional hearing on CFIUS and national security, where Rep. Lynch questions a witness about the scope of outbound investment restrictions on China.

statements.text: I just see us in a competition, you know, and I know China right now has full spectrum surveillance of its entire population. [...] The other aspect of this that I worry about is the power of AI [...] Mr. Timmons talked about the weaponization of weapon systems that would be completely autonomous [...] how can we, in the United States, in developing our AI policy, influence other countries, even in Europe, friendly, you know, and allies, other democracies, how do we make that happen?
statements.context: Congressional hearing or briefing on White House AI policy, December 6, 2023.

statements.text: In its final report, the bipartisan National Security Commission on Artificial Intelligence underscored that the preservation of U.S. leadership in global AI largely depends on our ability to present a democratic model, governing the use of AI for national security to the rest of the world.
statements.context: Congressional hearing (likely Oversight subcommittee) questioning an expert witness about U.S. AI governance and national security.

statements.text: how do we make sure that we protect consumers and investors if the AI algorithms are actually promoting uniformity or herding behavior—which, again, is a real threat—or the interpretability to understand what is actually going on with the AI system is not there? Wouldn't it make sense to have FSOC have undiluted power to be able to review activity like that in order to carry out their statutory mandate?
statements.context: House Financial Services Committee hearing on FSOC's designation framework, January 10, 2024.

statements.text: The only thing the opt outs will do, will is to prevent a new competitor from training new models to compete with them.
statements.context: Mr. Lynch speaks at a hearing on AI and the future of journalism, explaining why publisher opt-out mechanisms for AI training and output are impractical.

statements.text: Developers ought to be required to disclose essential information about the training, data, and safety of AI models to users and other companies.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI and the future of journalism, chaired by Senator Blumenthal.

statements.text: we urge Congress really to take immediate action to clarify that the use of publisher content for both training and the output of Gen AI is not covered by fair use. It must be licensed and compensated.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on AI and the future of journalism, with the chair pressing witnesses on the economic impact of AI on news publishers.

statements.text: Right. We won't have enough time for this, but maybe you can respond offline. Many of these asset management firms are actually purchasing—they are not building their own AI. They are purchasing it from an outside party, which is not subject to regulation. That creates a regulatory gap, and I am struggling with how to deal with that.
statements.context: Rep. Stephen Lynch questioning witnesses at a House Financial Services Committee hearing on FSOC's designation framework and innovation.

statements.text: I think quite simply, if Congress could clarify that the use of our content and other publisher content for training and output of AI models is not fair use, then the free market will take care of the rest.
statements.context: Witness testimony before a House subcommittee oversight hearing on AI and the future of journalism.

statements.text: we are beginning to see energy and resources being put into this effort, but one of the gaps is the availability of teachers in this discipline [...]
statements.context: House hearing titled "Toward an AI-Ready Workforce," where Rep. Stephen Lynch asks witnesses about building AI teacher capacity.

statements.text: I have some concerns. There are some opportunities, I think, to use artificial intelligence in a thoughtful way.
statements.context: Exchange during a House Financial Services Committee hearing with Treasury Secretary Janet Yellen on FSOC's annual report.

statements.text: As reported by the United States intelligence community in its Worldwide Threat Assessment recently, Russia, China, North Korea, and other state actors are continuing to conduct malign influence operations aimed at disseminating disinformation and magnifying U.S. societal divisions and interfering with the upcoming U.S. elections. [...] the introduction of generative AI sort of amplifies the possibilities of this exacerbated threat. [...] Dr. Turner Lee, what effect can we expect AI-generated deepfakes and misinformation to have on Americans' trust, their trust in the election process?
statements.context: House committee hearing on AI oversight, March 21, 2024, with Mr. Lynch questioning witnesses about AI-enabled election interference.

statements.text: Mr. L YNCH. I was thinking more about technology that could vet, you know, to look at. [...] are there proven methods that might allow us to uncover quickly, you know, a message that is not from its proposed source?
statements.context: House subcommittee hearing titled "White House Overreach on AI," where members question expert witnesses about AI policy.

statements.text: Clearly there are enormous potential benefits here, but there is also some concern around privacy and also the lack of explainability of some of these algorithms that are being used on the diagnosis or the predictive end.
statements.context: Congressional hearing on FDA oversight where Representative Lynch questions the agency about AI/ML medical device risks.

statements.text: The explosion of AI adoption across industries has raised serious questions about implications for financial access, employment, data privacy, and intellectual property. While AI has the potential to expand access to financial products, we need to ensure AI models are explainable, transparent, and do not lead to bias. Last, it is critical that the U.S. remain a leader in AI safety and security, and I look forward to continued collaboration with my colleagues as we further explore policy actions that are needed.
statements.context: Verbatim remarks by Rep. Stephen Lynch at a congressional hearing on AI applications in financial services and housing.

statements.text: On the one hand, it is great because with the help of AI, they might be able to compete with some of these big firms. [...] On the other hand, they are going to be relying on a third party for monitoring, for compliance, and for monitoring possible bias in their AI systems. How do we reconcile that, or do you think most of the firms now that provide AI as a service are able to properly monitor what is going on in these small banks or smaller financial firms?
statements.context: Congressional roundtable on AI applications in financial services and housing, featuring expert witnesses.

statements.text: For these large language models, it does look like because of the costs and the energy required, that there will just be a few big firms that will control that market.
statements.context: House Financial Services Committee hearing on AI applications in financial services and housing, where a member pushes back on a witness's claim about AI democratization.

statements.text: While they purged the Federal Government of expertise, Elon Musk and DOGE reportedly fed sensitive government data, including Americans' private personal information, into unvetted and unaccountable AI software. [...] They also reportedly deployed a Musk-owned generative AI chatbot called Grok to consume government data and assist with sensitive government decisions. Grok has even been deployed onto systems at the Department of Homeland Security, despite the fact that it has not been approved for use.
statements.context: Opening statement at a House Oversight and Government Reform Committee hearing on AI in the federal government, during which Rep. Lynch moved to subpoena Elon Musk.

statements.text: China has adopted an AI system that is total surveillance of their entire population there. It is non-democratic. It is quite oppressive. Their goal is to be able to surveil every single member of their society, know what they are doing, know what they are purchasing, and for oppressive reasons so that no one gets out of line. Can you talk about the need to, when we adopt, when we approve AI and choose the architecture for our AI, how important it is to make sure that transparency, that respecting privacy, independence, how important it is to have those elements of democracy itself ingrained and embodied in our AI models?
statements.context: Verbatim congressional hearing on the federal government in the age of artificial intelligence, with a representative questioning an expert witness.

statements.text: In view of these considerations, I am concerned by the Trump Administration's decision to rescind some of the commonsense Federal directives that sought to advance the safe and responsible development of artificial intelligence. This includes the reversal of an executive order directing all Federal agencies to enforce existing consumer protection laws and to develop additional regulatory safeguards against fraud, unintended bias, discrimination and privacy violations only when absolutely necessary.
statements.context: Opening statement at a House Financial Services Committee hearing on AI in the U.S. financial system, delivered by Rep. Stephen Lynch.

statements.text: So, interestingly enough, their sandbox has an ethical framework which begins with a principles-based approach so that there are elements of fairness and accountability, inclusivity, and it sets an ethical foundation for all AI projects.
statements.context: House Financial Services Committee hearing on AI in the U.S. financial system; Rep. Lynch opens with remarks relayed from a meeting with Anthropic's Jack Clark before questioning witnesses.

statements.text: One problem that I noticed in the Singapore model was the number of participants was limited, so it never scaled up. Some of the problems that we see with AI is when you get that scaleability. [...] Is there a way for us to—I know the auditing and review after the sandbox is ongoing, but is there any way we can sort of make sure that scaleability effect is implemented inside of a sandbox?
statements.context: Remarks delivered during a congressional hearing on AI in the U.S. financial system.

statements.text: It cannot—it says here it cannot be used as a means to circumvent legal and regulatory requirements, which is exactly what this bill is suggesting, that—that in adopting AI, they are allowing, or encouraging, ways of circumventing existing regulation in what are supposed to be a technology- neutral approach.
statements.context: Speaking at a House Financial Services Committee hearing on AI innovation in financial services, Rep. Lynch questions a witness about a bill's approach to AI regulatory sandboxes.

statements.text: We are inviting—we are inviting financial services companies as they deploy AI to choose which—which consumer investor protections, which soundness—safety and soundness regulations that they might want to avoid.
statements.context: Speaking at a Financial Services Committee hearing on AI innovation in financial services.

statements.text: However, as ranking member of the Subcommittee on Digital Assets, Financial Technology, and Artificial Intelligence in this Congress, I am concerned that some of the regulations—regulatory proposals before this committee not only fail to include adequate guardrails but they also invite the financial services industry in adopting AI to choose which consumer protection and investor protection and safety and soundness regulations that they would like to avoid, which is reckless and dangerous.
statements.context: Opening statement at a House Financial Services Committee hearing on AI innovation and regulation in financial services.
